The strips are about seven and a half sun long, roughly 23 centimetres, and about one centimetre in diameter. Beyond the bamboo strips the source does not record the material of the body, handle, cord decoration or any other part, nor say whether there is some other fixing structure. This section can therefore confirm only that the sounding body is bamboo; the other materials are not recorded.

小切子是日本傳統樂器，起源於富山縣南砺市五箇山地區。這種竹製打擊樂器在中世紀作為: Kokiriko is a Japanese traditional instrument, originating in the Gokayama area of Nanto, Toyama Prefecture. This bamboo percussion instrument was born in the Middle Ages as a tool of street performers, when entertainers called kokiriko often carried it for acrobatic and song-and-dance acts. By the Edo period kokiriko had gradually become an important accompanying instrument of folk music, used widely in folk song-and-dance performances such as the Kokiriko Bushi and the Kokiriko dance. The instrument is made of bamboo tube, which is why it is also written with the characters for 'bamboo tube'. Over time kokiriko developed from a mere street-performance tool into a formal folk art, and it was spread and preserved in folk festivals and traditional performances all over Japan, becoming an important part of Japanese traditional musical culture.

It is handed down in the Gokayama area of Toyama Prefecture, and also appears in the Ayakomai of Odani in Kashiwazaki, Niigata Prefecture. In the Gokayama kokiriko dance the lyrics sing out the length of the bamboo strips; another folk instrument, the sasara, is also used for accompaniment. Hōgashi performers walk while singing narrative songs, or strike the kokiriko at a crossroads; they are much loved by children.

Its timbre is light and clean, with the warm wooden quality typical of bamboo instruments, and it never loses its liveliness. The bamboo tube resonates as an idiophone, producing a clear, strongly rhythmic sound. Beside the dullness of drums the kokiriko is lighter and more nimble; beside a wooden fish or clappers its tone has more warmth and softness. In folk dance accompaniment the kokiriko's sound cuts through voices and singing and creates a cheerful, leaping atmosphere, which makes it an indispensable rhythmic instrument in Japanese folk performance.

Kokiriko is a Japanese idiophone made of two bamboo strips, each about seven and a half sun (about 23 cm) long and about one centimetre in diameter. The player holds one in each hand between the fingertips, rotating and striking them while singing and dancing. It is used for Japanese folk song and dance, for example Kokiriko Bushi; in the Gokayama area of Toyama Prefecture this folk song explicitly sings the length of the strips. Since the Middle Ages it has also been used by street performers, especially acrobats, striking and reciting while walking or standing at a crossroads; they are much loved by children.

Hold the body of the instrument and set it vibrating by striking, shaking, scraping or plucking it; different points and different amounts of force give different timbres. In practice, first confirm the correct holding position and master the basic way of sounding the instrument, then work on rhythm patterns and melody. Strike to sound it, and watch where you strike and how hard.
